articles.title: Birdfy’s new 4K feeder will teach you about the birds it identifies
articles.summary: The Birdfy Feeder Metal 2 features a chew-proof design to protect its seed stockpile from squirrels and other animals.
articles.body: Birdfy has announced a new version of its camera-equipped metal feeder with an upgraded camera to make you feel even closer to nature while staring at your phone from the sofa. The Birdfy Feeder Metal 2 has a similar design to the original, using metal panels that animals like squirrels can’t chew through to access its 1.8-liter stockpile of seeds. But it now features a 4K wide-angle camera — a big upgrade from the 1080P camera on the original — for capturing and streaming higher-res video. The Birdfy Feeder Metal 2 (4K) is launching today for $269.99. You’ll need to pay an optional monthly or annual subscription to access the company’s AI-powered Birdfy OrniSense system, which originally launched at CES 2026 with its Hum Bloom feeder for hummingbirds. The latest version can recognize more than 6,000 species and uses AI to generate a custom summary of facts and insights about the bird, instead of pointing users to a knowledge base like the previous iteration. Subscription pricing isn’t known yet, but for an extra $30, there’s also a $299.99 version of the feeder that comes with lifetime access to the AI features. (The subscription for the previous version costs $4.99 per month or $49 per year.) [Product: Birdfy Feeder Metal 2 (4K) | The new feeder’s Wi-Fi capabilities are also extended using an external antenna, so Birdfy claims it can be installed far from a home in a large yard without the need for additional signal extenders. But no matter where it’s installed, video is permanently capped at 20fps to keep livestreams running smoothly. Further streamlining installation is a built-in solar cell so the Birdfy Feeder Metal 2 (4K) doesn’t need access to power, and an IP66 weatherproof rating so you don’t need to worry about sheltering it from rain or other inclement weather.

articles.title: How often should you actually upgrade your iPhone?
articles.summary: Should you upgrade your iPhone this year? Here's what you need to know.
articles.body:
Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are now on store shelves, which means many people are wrestling with the question that comes around every year: Should you upgrade? Some people upgrade every year like clockwork, but they're absolutely in the minority. It turns out most of us — about 55% — only replace our phones every two to three years.

But with the costs going up on, well, everything these days , you might consider going another year with your current phone. And that's before you factor in Apple's $100 price increase on iPhone models, both old and new (thanks, RAMageddon ).

If you're conflicted on whether you should upgrade to the new iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max this year, here's what you might want to consider before pulling the trigger.

When do you need to upgrade your iPhone?

One thing Apple does exceptionally well is support old iPhones for a long time. In fact, iOS 27 , the latest version of the iPhone operating system, is supported on phones all the way back to 2019's iPhone 11 . A big part of the development for iOS 27 focused on speed and reliability improvements that should breathe new life into aging iPhones.

"As long as your phone can receive security updates, you are usually safe from a security perspective," Amrita Bhasin , the cofounder and CEO of Sotira , a reverse logistics company, told Yahoo Tech. "Unless your phone is pre-iPhone 11, you are generally safe to keep receiving iOS security updates for now."

However, there comes a time in every iPhone's life when it no longer receives updates, leaving you exposed to security vulnerabilities that are patched on newer devices. That's a major concern, and you should absolutely upgrade your iPhone to a newer model if your current one is left behind. After all, one of the best things you can do to stay safe online is download security and software updates as soon as possible. When your personal information and documents are at stake, it doesn't make sense to keep using an old device.

"Battery health is the primary driver in considering whether to upgrade a phone," Bhasin told Yahoo Tech. "If you feel like your phone needs to be charged multiple times per day and doesn't last a full day out, this may be a justifiable reason because battery effectiveness declines over time and use."

Fortunately, if you go to the "Battery" section of your iPhone's settings, you can see a report on its health and current maximum capacity. For example, my iPhone 16 Pro Max currently shows it's operating normally, with a total capacity of 91%. That's pretty good for a two-year-old device, but yours may be much more degraded if you're using something more than a few years old.

If you're struggling to make it through a whole day on a single charge, it might be time to consider an upgrade. That doesn't mean you have to choose the iPhone 18 Pro; an iPhone 16, 17 or Air can save you some money and perform just as well. If you're happy with your current phone, you could also try a battery replacement . After all, as Bhasin told us, "replacing batteries is cheaper than buying a whole new phone."

While iOS 27 definitely feels snappier than iOS 26, it might not provide enough of a lift for older phones like the iPhone 11 and 12. The A20 Pro chip in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the A19 chips from last year's models, both offer significant performance and efficiency improvements over those in older iPhones. This metric can be subjective, but an upgrade may be worth it if you frequently find yourself frustrated by how long your phone takes to complete simple tasks.

Should you upgrade if you have an iPhone 16 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro?

Unless you're particularly excited about new camera features or slight design tweaks, the upgrade from an iPhone 16 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro likely isn't worth it. Here's a brief look at what the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max improve over the two most recent models.

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max vs. iPhone 16 Pro and Pro Max

Three 48MP rear cameras with variable aperture on one.

A smaller Dynamic Island on the front display

Improved vapor chamber cooling for better sustained performance.

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max

If you have an iPhone 16 Pro or Pro Max, you'll feel the upgrade a little more, thanks to the improved cooling and more RAM. However, the upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max is unlikely to feel much different, especially with both phones featuring largely the same design (down to the same dimensions). If you're happy with your current phone, it might be worth waiting until the 2027 iPhone, especially with rumors of a major redesign for the device's 20th anniversary.

If your iPhone is no longer receiving security updates, then you should definitely upgrade to one that does. While that may be the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, it doesn't have to be. Finding a well-maintained, used iPhone 15 or 16 could be the right choice. Or, you can go directly to Apple and get something a little newer.

If your battery is your main concern, an upgrade could be your ticket to living without worrying about where you'll get your next charge. However, you can just as easily pay Apple for a battery replacement and save quite a bit of money. Currently, replacements cost $100 for an iPhone 15 Pro Max and are even cheaper for older models.

Bhasim told us she encourages everyone to use their phones as long as possible, or at least until battery life and performance affect day-to-day use. "Electronics waste is a significant climate problem and a lot of excess or used electronics unfortunately end up in the landfill," she told us. "Resist pressure to upgrade simply because there is a new option and only upgrade when your existing devices do not have the same utility day to day."

articles.title: Google lança notebook com IA para competir com MacBooks; veja fotos e preço | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova linha de notebooks custa a partir de US$ 899 e reúne ferramentas de inteligência artificial Gemini, processadores Intel ou Qualcomm e integração com celulares Android.
articles.summary: Nova linha de notebooks custa a partir de US$ 899 e reúne ferramentas de inteligência artificial Gemini, processadores Intel ou Qualcomm e integração com celulares Android.
articles.body:
Google lança Googlebook, um laptop que compete com os computadores da Apple. — Foto: Divulgação/Google

O Google abriu nesta segunda-feira (21) a pré-venda do Googlebook, sua nova linha de notebooks premium voltada para usuários de Android.

Os aparelhos têm recursos de inteligência artificial Gemini e preços a partir de US$ 899 (R$ 4.584,9).

Os primeiros modelos serão produzidos por Acer , Asus , Dell , HP e Lenovo . Eles terão processadores Intel ou Qualcomm e bateria com autonomia de até 14 horas , segundo o Google.

A nova linha chega em um momento de maior concorrência no mercado de notebooks. A Apple avançou no segmento de aparelhos mais acessíveis com o MacBook Neo, que custa a partir de US$ 699 (R$ 3.564,9).

Há anos, os fabricantes de Chromebooks disputam esse público, principalmente estudantes e consumidores que buscam aparelhos mais baratos e simples.

Com o Googlebook, o Google leva essa proposta para notebooks premium, combinando hardware mais potente, recursos de inteligência artificial e uma integração maior com o sistema Android.

Ferramentas para ajudar o usuário a escrever e organizar textos;

Fazer perguntas sobre o conteúdo que aparece na tela; e

Retomar, no notebook, tarefas iniciadas em um celular Android.

O Googlebook é a mais recente tentativa da empresa de apresentar um produto de destaque baseado no ChromeOS. Antes dele, o Google lançou o Pixelbook, em 2017, e o Pixelbook Go, em 2019.

Aplicativos, navegador e ferramentas para trabalho

O Googlebook combina o navegador Chrome para computadores, com suporte a extensões, com aplicativos disponíveis na Play Store .

Entre os programas que podem ser usados no computador estão Adobe Photoshop , Adobe Lightroom e CapCut . O aparelho também permite acessar serviços de streaming como Netflix e HBO Max , inclusive com suporte à visualização offline.

Para jogos, o Googlebook oferece acesso a milhares de títulos para Android e inclui um ano de assinatura do GeForce NOW em cada compra.

O computador também foi pensado para desenvolvedores. O Googlebook inclui o Antigravity , plataforma de desenvolvimento de agentes de inteligência artificial do Google, que permite criar, testar e colocar aplicativos em funcionamento diretamente no dispositivo.

Há ainda um ambiente de terminal para executar ferramentas de desenvolvimento, como Claude Code e Antigravity CLI.

As pré-vendas já estão abertas nos Estados Unidos. Os aparelhos começam a chegar às lojas em 4 de outubro nos EUA e em 5 de outubro no Canadá, Reino Unido, Irlanda, França, Alemanha e Austrália.

articles.title: I got to see Google’s wild ideas about the future of laptops
articles.summary: Google is launching its Googlebooks on October 4th, starting at $899. The Android-based laptops have some interesting ideas about how a laptop interacts with a phone.
articles.body: There are a few things about using a Googlebook that immediately feel just right. The hardware is polished (since it’s based on current laptops). The OS is familiar (if you’ve ever used a Chromebook). But most impressive, it integrates your Android phone with your PC so they feel more like one device. It’s the culmination of a series of new ideas that blur the two devices together. After my first look, I went from doubtful to excited by the prospect of Google pulling it all off. After an initial bare-bones announcement in May, Google is finally launching Googlebooks — its new line of Android-based laptops. The initial five Googlebook models from Dell, Lenovo, HP, Acer, and Asus all launch October 4th, with preorders available now and starting prices ranging from $899 to $1,299. So what are Googlebooks? In a nutshell, they’re laptops running a new operating system that’s a blend of Chromebooks and Android — with a whole lot of Gemini AI stuff built in. They look quite like Chromebooks, but with Android’s Material Three Expressive UI stylings on the software side and higher-end materials for hardware. There doesn’t seem to be a baseline spec for Googlebooks, but at launch they’re all thin-and-light laptops ranging from 13 inches to 15 inches with 16GB of RAM or more, touchscreen displays (most of them OLED), metal chassis, backlit keyboards, either fingerprint or facial recognition unlocking (or both), and a Google-y Glowbar light strip on their lids. [Image: The launch lineup for Googlebooks. Powering the initial lineup of Googlebooks are Intel Core Ultra Series 3 “Panther Lake” and Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite chips, with MediaTek options expected to come later. While the first wave of Googlebooks are similarly sized and all have “Googlebook” in their name, there are some variations: haptic or mechanical trackpads, port offerings, even a 2-in-1 convertible. Check out our roundup of all the hardware here. I spent a bit of time prodding all the Googlebooks during my demos, and each one felt pretty nice. They each have their own unique qualities: The Asus was incredibly lightweight; the Lenovo has plenty of ports and an optional mouse with a matching Glowbar light; the Acer’s convertible form factor allows some tablet-like use (and it’s pretty affordable for a Panther Lake laptop). The HP had a great-looking screen and a latticeless keyboard I surprisingly didn’t hate, and the Dell is basically a gold XPS 13 (which is excellent) but with a different chip. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: But everything really special about Googlebooks comes down to software. They run Googlebook OS, which is built with the native Android stack atop a Linux kernel and supports both x86 and Arm architectures (as implied by the chip offerings). It’s an Android desktop interface that runs Android apps and feels much like ChromeOS, but it’s got some handy features when paired with an Android phone. You can cast apps from an Android phone directly to a Googlebook, even without touching your phone. Googlebooks essentially have two app drawers: a G-logo start menu for installed Googlebook apps and a second one beside it that pulls up mobile apps from your phone. Click a phone app and you can fully use that app with the mouse and keyboard or the Googlebook’s touchscreen. It’s a bit like iPhone Mirroring on macOS, but the apps are individually extracted to the desktop OS instead of showing your whole phone interface. [Image: [Image: Googlebooks also have a nifty feature called Continue On where the icons of apps you’re currently using on your phone appear in the bottom bar — allowing you to click it on the laptop and hand it off to the Googlebook. These app handoffs can transition to a native app or a web app, depending on how developers have programmed it. A Google rep informed me at my in-person briefing that Continue On is fairly simple for Android developers to add to their apps, and casting apps to a Googlebook doesn’t require anything extra. The other big way Googlebooks interact with an Android phone is Quick Access, allowing you to see and access all the files stored on your phone right in the desktop Files app. The paired Android phone is listed in the sidebar of a Googlebook’s Files window, just like any other drive or home folder, and you can directly search it and share files from it without physically picking up your phone. This is pretty handy stuff, but of course it all requires you running an Android phone. If you have an iPhone then you’re limited to a Link to iOS app that just does some message syncing and replying. [Image: [Image: As Google first showed in May, the Googlebook mouse cursor is called a Magic Pointer — allowing you to wiggle it to summon Gemini. Doing so allows you to ask Gemini questions or have it look at things on your screen to get further info. One of Google’s live demos was asking Gemini “Is this legit?” on a Spotify account authentication email, or adding a multi-week exercise routine for marathon training to a Google Calendar. Some tasks run locally, while many will go up to Gemini in the cloud — and it wasn’t clear when that was happening during any of Google’s demos. Googlebooks also have recent Android features like Create My Widget (for creating custom widgets from natural-language prompts) and Rambler (speech transcription that can parse stream-of-consciousness-like wordiness). And while thin-and-light laptops aren’t really built for gaming, since Googlebooks run Android they work with 20,000 games at launch. Many of these are free-to-play mobile games with microtransactions, of course, but the Play Store does have many indie titles that should play fine on a laptop. I briefly demoed a Googlebook running Dead Cells and Balatro — indie staples that are well worth playing on any platform. But it was also jarring to see a demo of Asphalt Legends offer me the option to watch a post-race ad for an in-game currency reward. That felt icky and weird on a laptop. But when it comes to mainline gaming, Nvidia’s GeForce Now service is also coming to Googlebooks, and the first year is free with one of Google’s new laptops. [Image: [Image: A big draw of Googlebooks is that by being Android-based they can follow software developments that move at a much quicker pace than ChromeOS. Chromebooks will continue on, especially for education use where they’re widely adopted, but it’s pretty easy to feel like their days are numbered as the focus shifts to Googlebooks. Just like Chromebooks, Google is promising Googlebooks will get 10 years of OS support. I kept asking who Googlebooks are for during Google’s media briefing, and Android president Sameer Samat told me they’re aimed at users who own a phone like a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 who don’t particularly want to use Windows or a Mac. Googlebooks’ initial prices completely overlook direct competition with the MacBook Neo (at least for now), but considering the state of Windows 11 and frequently voiced frustrations with Microsoft (I see you, Verge commenters), another competitor in the space could help mix things up. [Image: [Image: One thing I found comforting was the work Google put into flagging apps as desktop-compatible in the Play Store. Kind of like how Valve verifies games for Steam Deck and Steam Machine compatibility, Google has three designations for Play Store apps on Googlebooks: Made for desktop, Optimized for desktop, or Better on the website. It’s cool to see an “Optimized for desktop” version of Lightroom I can install on a Google laptop, though I know it’s the mobile version and not the Lightroom Classic I regularly use on Windows and macOS. But while that hints at Google taking this initiative pretty seriously, and all the Android integration tricks seem cool, there are many open questions for Google and its new OS that remain to be answered. * Even if Chromebooks continue on strictly for education, what will happen as that software ages with the development attention turned to Googlebooks? * Do people want to trust Google with their whole computer these days? * Do people want a laptop built with Gemini in mind? There’s an ongoing AI backlash, and Googlebooks puts Gemini at the forefront — even in the cursor. * Will developers like Adobe further optimize their mobile creative apps for desktop use? Or bring desktop-only apps like Lightroom Classic to Android? (Please?) * Are these laptops ready for showtime? Not to get too inside baseball, but Google isn’t sending out review units ahead of the launch. And some OEM reps told me they just got the hardware shortly before our briefing — deferring all software questions to Google. Maybe that’s no big deal, but it doesn’t instill much confidence. * What will future cheaper Googlebooks look and feel like? And just how cheap (or expensive) might they get — especially in the age of RAMageddon? After seeing what Googlebooks can do, I went from having no idea why they even exist to feeling at least adequately whelmed and looking forward to seeing some new ideas and competition in the laptop space (even if it might be just another Trojan horse for Gemini). It’s not every day we get a new player in the desktop operating system and laptop spaces. There seems to be a higher ceiling of potential with Googlebooks than there was with Chromebooks, along with some cool features, but Google has a lot to prove at higher prices than people are used to paying for its laptops. Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: The long dream of the Googlebook
articles.summary: By merging ChromeOS and Android, Google has found a new kind of laptop that it thinks can compete with Mac and Windows.
articles.body: In late 2010, an up-and-coming Google executive named Sundar Pichai took the stage in front of a bunch of reporters and explained that Google had a big new idea about laptops. In the future, he said, the only thing you’d need on your computer was a web browser — that was where all your apps, data, and connections would live going forward. Your computer didn’t need much storage, Pichai explained, or any fancy hardware, because the cloud would do the work. The software designed for these new laptops, Chrome OS, was an enormous bet that the web would eventually overtake everything. Chrome OS (which eventually became ChromeOS) has been, in many ways, a huge hit. But the computer currently on Rick Osterloh’s desk isn’t a Chromebook. Osterloh is Google’s head of hardware and devices, and the sleek, slim device he’s tapping on as he joins our Google Meet is a 13-inch Dell clamshell with decidedly un-Chromebook specs: 16 gigs of RAM, a cutting-edge Qualcomm processor, a light and thin and MacBook-ish metallic look. It’s called the XPS Googlebook, and it’s one of five new devices running Googlebook OS, Google’s latest big idea about computers. At first blush, Googlebooks feel like classic Google in a bad way: yet another operating system, yet another brand, yet another thing destined for the Google graveyard. But Osterloh sees it differently. He greenlit the whole project in part because he saw it as “the ultimate focusing move” for Google. For a long time, he says, Google has built, maintained, and shipped two operating systems. ChromeOS stayed on laptops, while Android conquered phones and tablets and TVs and cars and everything else. Slowly but surely, Google has built Android into a familiar interface and a large app ecosystem across all those devices. Except for laptops. [Image: It’s your computer. It’s your phone. It’s your phone-puter! Meanwhile, Google became convinced that the advent of AI might change the way we use computers forever — but might not need to change the computers themselves. Osterloh says he has tables full of wheel-reinventing prototypes, and of course the company is betting big on things like smart glasses, but high-end PCs, which have the power needed to run AI models for coding, dictation, and more, have been a surprise winner of the AI revolution so far. (Just ask Apple, which has seen AI enthusiasts buy high-end Macs in huge volume.) “I think laptops are one of those resonant form factors,” Osterloh says. “It’s an established category that’s incredibly useful for productivity and apps, and it’s going to be really hard to replace that.” Those two ideas together — Android’s dominance and the rise of AI — tell the whole story of Googlebook. There are a lot of bets inside of the Googlebook project, both about what we do on computers and how we’ll do it going forward, but maybe the most surprising is Google’s commitment to building kickass laptops. A generation ago, then-CEO Eric Schmidt argued that the future was “disposable” hardware, that devices wouldn’t matter as the internet took over. Googlebooks represent Google’s growing belief that devices matter more than ever. And that a good laptop is worth paying for. The Googlebook project started in earnest a couple of years ago, but some of the ideas have been floating around much longer. Rumors and reports of a ChromeOS-Android merger have been around for more than a decade, and Google has tried various ways to bring the two operating systems into harmony. The company spent years programming ChromeOS to be able to run Android apps (and even Windows apps), but never nailed the integration. For years, a project called Fuchsia looked like the combination users had been waiting for, but that petered out into a smart home-specific project. In early 2024, though, a couple of Googlers asked a new question: What if, instead of trying to bring Android apps to ChromeOS, we brought the best of ChromeOS to Android? They weren’t the first people to ask that question, but they were the first to time it right. “The key thing that had changed,” says Prajakta Gudadhe, Google’s VP of engineering for laptops and tablets, “was just the rapid pace of evolution that Android itself has gone under.” For so many years, Android was a phone operating system that was sometimes hamfistedly shoved into other devices. But Gudadhe felt like Android had finally matured into something truly cross-platform. Developers had begun to embrace multiple screen sizes and orientations, and the Android team at Google had changed the way they built the operating system. “Android at that time was serving multiple form factors, from phones to wearables to TVs to autos,” Gudadhe says, “and because of that they just had to invest in a much more modular stack that could support this diversity.” [Image: Googlebooks will be able to open apps from your Android phone. What that meant in practice was that it might finally be possible to build an Android laptop that could natively run the universe of Android apps, without looking and working like a grossly oversized Android phone. By combining base Android technology with some of the best features of ChromeOS — excellent multitasking and multi-window support, fast boot times, easy software updates — Google could have the best of both worlds. The idea became a memo proposing a new laptop OS, which was excitedly received by Google leadership, and Project Aluminium was born. (To be clear: It is A-lu-min-i-um, not aluminum, and there was a swear jar in the office for people who dared to pronounce it the American way.) In addition to the technical underpinnings, the Aluminium pitch included a couple of big ideas about the future of laptops. The first was that more and more users were starting their computing journey with Android devices, and thus were expecting all their other computers to both interact with and even look like their Android phones. They wanted widgets, homescreens, notification shades, and customization options. They also wanted all their apps on their laptop, and their data in perfect sync all the time. That became one of the core tenets of the operating system — perfect integration with Android devices. (iPhone owners were, and are, mostly out of luck on this front.) The team was also convinced that Gemini and other AI tools were part of the future of computing, and that they should be built into the operating system and not just a separate app. The advent of vibe coding meant people might want to build their own software, in a terminal or with the help of on-device agents, and would surely want easier ways to get it running on their devices. But even little things about computer use felt ripe for AI change. “The mouse pointer? That thing seems pretty stupid,” says Alexander Kuscher, Google’s senior director of product management for laptops and tablets, just naming one example. Your cursor represents your attention, and moves around with your brain and your eyes, so why can’t your computer just see and respond to it? “I’m copying and pasting stuff all over the place, and typing to chatbots that don’t give me the ability to just express my needs with the mouse pointer.” That thinking became one of the most novel features of Googlebook OS, Magic Pointer, which lets you invoke your AI bot just by wiggling your cursor over an image or a bit of text. The idea, Kuscher said, was to “not change the ergonomics [of a laptop], but to make sure we take care of people coming from the ecosystem, living in an AI world.” [Image: Running, and making, Android apps is core to Googlebook. As the Aluminium team started working on an AI-centric, Android-powered laptop, they began discovering problems — and other teams at Google trying to solve them. “One is Android Automotive, which cares a lot about multi-user,” Kuscher says. “They need fast user switching because different people get in the car. We were like, oh, me too!” They found folks on the Android Wear team working on improving the Bluetooth stack for better accessory connectivity, and people on the XR team thinking about multi-window support for Android. This is the focusing that gets Osterloh excited. The well-earned stereotype about Google is that nobody ever talks to anybody else, and so the company ships a thousand slightly different messaging apps, reminders systems, and AI subscriptions. In that vein, the Aluminium team could have come up with new ideas about everything and baked them all into ChromeOS; what they did instead was integrate so many disparate ideas about Android into a single platform. Even the ultimate name of the devices and the software, Googlebook and Googlebook OS, hint at the extent to which Google hopes Aluminium brings everything Google-y together in one place. “We realized pretty quickly that this is about the whole Google experience,” Kuscher says. “If you have a phone that runs Google, and a car, and a laptop, that’s what this is about.” (The naming here is a delightful bit of Google chaos, by the way. Googlebooks run Googlebook OS, which is mostly Android, but with some ChromeOS trappings thrown in. Get it? Me neither. They’re Android laptops.) [Image: Android phones are treated like another drive in the file system. It became very clear to the Googlebook team that this operating system was going to ask a lot of the hardware it ran on. All the system-level AI would need enough processing power and memory to feel seamless, of course, but it went further than that. “We didn’t want to have Magic Pointer, and then it’s really hard on your trackpad to actually use it,” says Kuscher. “That’s just incongruent.” Likewise, what good is letting you build software with a prompt if the keyboard is awful to type on or the battery dies before it’s done? If the screen is too small, or too low-res, nobody will want to use it instead of their phone. For a Googlebook to be even a little bit worthwhile, the hardware would need to be great. From the beginning, Osterloh says, Google wanted to build an ecosystem of Googlebooks. The company began reaching out to PC makers, chip companies, and even phone manufacturers, all with roughly the same pitch: You’ve already been making either great laptops, great Android devices, or both, and now we’re putting the whole puzzle together. For a PC industry always looking for Windows competition and increasingly interested in building ecosystems of products to compete with Apple, the pitch worked: Google is starting with five devices from five partners — Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo — and Osterloh says there are many other partners waiting in the wings. Potentially including Google’s own Pixel team. The first five devices, he said, are merely the ones that are ready now. And he says partners are clamoring to be next. The harder group to convince of this whole thing? Users. For all their success in education and elsewhere, Chromebooks never really caught on as personal computers. That’s largely Google’s fault, and largely for two reasons: because Google never successfully convinced people that all they needed was a web browser, and because Google and its partners spent so many years making and marketing crappy computers. Early Chromebook commercials were, in fact, explicitly anti-hardware: They showed people lighting their laptops on fire and throwing them into rivers, because who cared about the device when everything was in the cloud? As a result, even when Google and its partners have made high-end Chromebooks, like the terrific Pixelbook, they failed to convince anyone that they were worth the money. The first lineup of Googlebooks will cost between $899 and $1,299, which puts them squarely in competition with devices like the MacBook Air. Osterloh says he thinks Googlebooks will eventually reach other form factors and lower prices, but seems unfazed by the task of convincing people to spend top dollar on a Google laptop. For one thing, he thinks the increasing popularity of AI has made people more willing to buy high-end computers in general, and has maybe even increased the importance of laptops and desktops. “I still fundamentally believe it will always be your central computer,” he says. “The thing that connects you to networks, that has the primary brain, the important screen for entertainment and productivity.” But more than that, he agrees that this kind of hardware, and this kind of price tag, are simply what it requires to do Googlebooks well. And Google definitely won’t get a third chance to convince you it’s right about laptops. [Image: Googlebooks have some fun features like a glowing bar, but mostly they’re laptops. When Google first announced the Googlebook concept in May, it was heavily focused on AI and Gemini. But the work that led to Googlebooks goes back much further than the company’s current obsession with LLMs, and is about more than Google’s chatbot. In some ways, Osterloh says, the whole history of Android has led up to the launch of Googlebooks. Their first job, as he sees it, is to “run the applications you know how to use and sync really well with all your Android usage and applications and devices that you’ve connected to it. And it just happens to be an awesome laptop.” Sixteen years ago, Google shipped a laptop for the internet age. Now it’s trying to build one for the mobile era that has already come, and the AI-centric one that’s still forming. Getting it right will require marshaling nearly everything Google does well — and the best devices it has ever made. It will also require proving to users that they need a computer that’s more like their phone, and more connected to their AI ecosystem. None of that is a given; it might be an even bigger leap than trying to move your laptop to the web. But if Google’s bet pays off, our cursors might never wiggle the same way again.

articles.title: Taylor Frankie Paul Steps Away From ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ After Allegedly Failing Court-Ordered Drug Test, Citing ‘Disgusting’ Bullying From Castmates
articles.summary: Though Taylor Frankie Paul had just set her return to “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” she says she has decided to step away from the Hulu reality show af...
articles.body:
Though Taylor Frankie Paul had just set her return to "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives," she says she has decided to step away from the Hulu reality show after the latest development in her months-long legal scandal with the fathers of her children.

In a post on Instagram on Monday, Paul wrote that her "gratitude goes out to all the networks that supported me throughout this and gave me the chance to return. However I don't desire to move forward like this." She then lashed out at her "Mormon Wives" castmates, saying they'd engaged in a "pile on" — she wrote that "laughing about my kids is disgusting." Since Season 5 of the show premiered on Sept. 10, the "Mormon Wives" cast, which has been filming Season 6 without Paul since July, have been going back and forth ceaselessly on social media.

Sources told Variety last week that, as reported by TMZ , Paul allegedly failed a recent drug test ordered by a Utah court during her ongoing custody battles with her ex-boyfriend, Dakota Mortensen, which whom she shares one son, and her ex-husband, Tate Paul, with whom she shares a son and daughter. Whether Disney and Hulu would have moved forward with Paul after the failed drug test is now a question that will never be answered.

Paul did not address the drug test allegations in her Instagram post. Neither Hulu nor representatives for Paul immediately responded to a request for comment.

Paul was required to take the drug test after a court ruling in July, but her results were put under a protective order, preventing them from being shared outside of those directly involved in the case. Her ex-husband filed documents asking the court to unseal the results on Aug. 13, but they were not public until TMZ's reporting.

Both custody battles began after an explosion in Paul and Mortensen's relationship back in March, when production on "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives" paused due to a police investigation into domestic violence allegations the two made against each other. Soon after, TMZ published video from a separate incident between them, which showed Paul in a violent altercation with Mortensen and throwing a chair while one of her children was nearby. That prompted Disney to unschedule the premiere of "The Bachelorette" Season 22 , which featured Paul as the star. With additional allegations made by both Paul and Mortensen, a court granted them mutual restraining orders, but neither of them faced charges.

The scandal has ricocheted onto all involved with "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives," with several online feuds occurring among cast members in the months leading up to the Sept. 10 release of Season 5. Shortly after Season 5 was released, Mikayla Matthews announced she had left the show midway through filming Season 6. She later clarified that she was leaving because of a moral objection to Paul's return . (To that end, Paul wrote on Monday, "I originally was willing to be removed to let them all continue on with less stress and I'm back to that point.") Cast members Mayci Neeley and Layla Taylor both indicated they were also unsure about their futures on the show after the news. Whitney Leavitt had already announced her decision to leave the show months ago, citing her budding acting career.

Paul's post on Monday concluded with this bit, directed toward her former #MomTok sorority: "I treated production and crew with respect always, in fact they are ones who checked on me throughout this. I agree it's to the point of bullying for months now. What makes it harder to take in is some of these parents have made mistakes that would result in the same judgement I'm receiving yet pointing a finger. However it's a pleasure to remove myself so they can continue, because I've almost convinced myself I'm deserving of all this pain and to a certain degree absolutely this is consequences of my actions. My question has been how much suffering and scrutiny is going to be enough…I'm just relieved to be out."

articles.title: GOP leaders face challenge from lame-duck lawmakers in both parties
articles.summary: Lame-duck lawmakers in the lower chamber are going out with guns blazing. In a series of extraordinary moves ahead of the midterms, soon-to-depart members forced votes on long-shot impeachments, carried discharge petitions over the top, and hopped the aisle to help the opposing party secure legislative wins — all in defiance of their own leaders.…
articles.body:
Lame-duck lawmakers in the lower chamber are going out with guns blazing.

In a series of extraordinary moves ahead of the midterms, soon-to-depart members forced votes on long-shot impeachments, carried discharge petitions over the top, and hopped the aisle to help the opposing party secure legislative wins — all in defiance of their own leaders.

The agitators hail from different parties; they’re pushing different issues; and they have wildly different motivations for going rogue. But they all have at least two things in common: They won’t be back next year, and they have nothing to lose.

They could also make life difficult for leaders on both sides of the aisle in the postelection session, when Congress must extend government funding or trigger a shutdown, and GOP leaders will be scrambling to secure a few final victories before the year ends.

The dynamics are in a way a mirror of the Senate, where a small handful of departing GOP lawmakers have also asserted a newfound independence given their lame-duck status. Dubbed the “YOLO” caucus, that group includes Sens. John Cornyn (Texas) and Bill Cassidy (La.), both of whom lost primary contests to President Trump-backed Republicans this summer, as well as Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.), who announced his retirement plans last year amid a clash with Trump over the president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The challenge for House GOP leaders will be front and center in the earliest days of Congress’s return to Washington, which is scheduled for Nov. 9, when they’ll have to contend immediately with a resolution to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

That proposal is being pushed by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), a longtime Trump critic whose crusade against the administration has only escalated since he lost his primary to a MAGA challenger who was backed by Trump and pledged his loyalty to the president. (Separately, Massie is also championing a discharge petition on legislation that would force the Justice Department to release all its files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex trafficker who was once good friends with Trump.)

Massie is well known in the Capitol for opposing foreign interventions, including the Iran war, which he considers illegal because it lacks congressional approval. But he still surprised Washington last week when he unveiled eight impeachment articles against Hegseth, with half of them related to how the Pentagon has conducted that conflict.

The move not only caught GOP leaders off guard but also put them in a bind. The Iran war is unpopular with voters, and a vote on Hegseth would have put some vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot as they fight to retain control of the House in the midterms. GOP leaders avoided that vote by cutting the legislative calendar a day short to get lawmakers out of Washington and on the campaign trail — a move that quickly prompted accusations from Massie and Democrats that Republican leaders fled to dodge a difficult issue.

“They shut down the Legislative Branch of the United States of America because I was outmaneuvering the Speaker to expose a global sex trafficking ring and impeach a rogue cabinet secretary,” Massie wrote Friday on the social platform X. “It was the only way they could stop me.”

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has dismissed that narrative as “ridiculous,” portraying Massie’s move as a “publicity stunt by someone who wants attention.” But the Speaker has no power to stop the Hegseth vote from happening in the lame-duck period. And there’s also a real chance that Massie’s push to release the Epstein files will hit the floor after the election.

That’s because he and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) say they have enough Republican support to meet the 218-signature threshold to force a vote on the files, even against the wishes of the GOP leaders who control the chamber. Massie said it’s two other lame-duck lawmakers — Reps. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) and Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) — who have helped to put the petition over the top.

“When we return from recess that @SpeakerJohnson imposed until the election, @RepRoKhanna & I will have 218 names required to force a vote!” Massie wrote on X.

Mace, who lost her bid for governor this summer, also signed a separate discharge petition just before the break on legislation expanding benefits for disabled veterans. In doing so, she became the 218th signature on the petition, paving the way for a potential vote on the legislation in the lame-duck period.

“We signed this discharge petition because enough is enough,” Mace said in a statement.

Norman, meanwhile, is making waves in other ways. He ran unsuccessfully to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), and since then he has voted on several occasions against GOP rules, including two episodes in which GOP leaders had to lean on a pair of centrist Democrats to get the underlying legislation to the floor. (Texas GOP Rep. Chip Roy, yet another lame-duck lawmaker who lost his run for Texas attorney general, opposed one of those rules.)

Norman also bashed Republican leaders for cutting September’s legislative session short. “The Founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid,” he wrote on X.

Democrats are hardly immune from the trend.

Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), who is retiring at the end of the term, has crossed the aisle in two high-profile cases to help Johnson advance the Republicans’ late-campaign legislative agenda, even as some of those bills were designed to hurt vulnerable Democrats in November. In both cases, he was joined by Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.), who’s facing a tough reelection contest in November.

The defections have infuriated fellow Democrats — leaders and rank-and-file members alike — who are fighting to keep their message squarely on the high cost of living under Trump’s second term but continue to face questions about disunity within their own ranks.

“There’s no excuse for it, really,” Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) said.

Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) is on a tear of his own. Green, a 22-year House veteran who lost his primary over the summer after Texas’s redistricting, has led the charge for Trump’s impeachment going back to the president’s first term. Those efforts have been cheered by liberals, who want Democrats to fight harder against the administration but have not always been welcomed by leadership.

That was certainly the case when Green forced a Trump impeachment resolution to the floor last week, agitating many of his Democratic colleagues who want to focus squarely on the volatile economy.

All the top Democratic leaders voted “present” and distanced themselves from the effort.

“This is something, oftentimes, I think the right-wing media wants us to talk about,” Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the head of the House Democratic Caucus, said of impeaching Trump.

“But it’s not anything that is top of the agenda for House Democrats.”

images.caption: Members leave the House Chamber at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., following the last votes of the week on Sept. 16, 2026. The House will return following the midterm elections in November.
